docs.title: Law by AI
docs.text: AI-powered platform for legal document processing, retrieval, and analysis.

docs.title: 🎯 Vision
docs.text: Law by AI aims to make legal information accessible, searchable, and actionable through modern AI techniques — from document ingestion and semantic search to change tracking and knowledge graph exploration.

docs.text: This project is in early implementation. The Intention doc captures our scope, the Architecture doc details the direct-integration design, and the project board tracks all active work across 7 milestones.

docs.title: System Architecture
docs.text: Status: Draft (Rev. 2) — reflects the revised architecture plan defined in the Intention doc and tracked as ADRs in the ADR Register below.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Law by AI is a self-hosted, multi-tenant platform for legal document ingestion, processing, retrieval, and analysis. PostgreSQL is a direct, hardcoded integration (ADR-0014); the protocol-based plugin system is deprecated and each backend will become a direct dependency.

All services run under Docker-Compose and communicate over the internal network.

Efficiency budget: the whole stack must run fast on ~4–6 GB RAM with a small local model (SLM). This constrains model choices, integrations, and task design.

docs.title: Architecture Principles
docs.text:
1. Direct integrations — PostgreSQL (and later each store/model) is a hardcoded dependency, not a swappable plugin. (ADR-0014)
  2. Single provider per concern — one relational store, one graph store, one vector store; avoid multi-backend abstractions a one-person project cannot maintain.
  3. Efficiency first — the RAM/SLM budget governs every decision.
  4. Observable by default — structlog JSON + OTel metrics/traces, shipped via Grafana Alloy → Grafana Cloud, anonymized. (ADR-0005)
  5. Tenant-safe by construction — multi-tenant isolation with automated leak tests. (ADR-0003)
  6. Resilient tasks — Celery tasks with retry policies and in-DB failure monitoring. (ADR-0006)

docs.title: PostgreSQL Integration (hardcoded, ADR-0014)
docs.text: PostgreSQL is the single relational store, accessed directly via PostgreSQLStore (plugins/relational_db/postgres.py) — no protocol indirection. Schema is managed by Alembic migrations; see Migrations for commands.

docs.title: Deprecated plugin scaffolding
docs.text:
The remaining six plugin types (VectorDB, GraphDB, KnowledgeSource, Embedding, LLM, Reranking) are deprecated per ADR-0014. Their protocols, PluginManager, and config/plugins.yaml stay in the tree for now but are phased out as each backend becomes a direct integration. config/plugins.yaml has no active registrations.

classDiagram
    class VectorDBPlugin {
        <<protocol>>
        +upsert_embeddings()
        +search_embeddings()
        +delete_embeddings()
        +create_collection()
        +delete_collection()
    }
    class GraphDBPlugin {
        <<protocol>>
        +add_node()
        +add_edge()
        +get_related_nodes()
        +get_node()
        +delete_node()
        +delete_edge()
        +get_all_nodes()
        +get_all_edges()
    }
    class KnowledgeSourcePlugin {
        <<protocol>>
        +fetch()
        +validate_config()
        +list_sources()
    }
    class EmbeddingPlugin {
        <<protocol>>
        +generate_embeddings()
        +get_model_info()
        +get_embedding_dimension()
    }
    class LLMPlugin {
        <<protocol>>
        +generate_response()
        +step_back_prompt()
        +generate_rag_query()
        +traverse_graph()
    }
    class RerankingPlugin {
        <<protocol>>
        +rerank()
    }

Future direction (ADR-0014): each of these becomes a direct integration:

  • Graph: Neo4j AuraDB Free (cloud-managed). (ADR-0002)
  • Vector: Qdrant.
  • Knowledge sources: web/git/filesystem ETL modules.
  • Embedding: a dedicated embedding provider (may differ from the LLM provider).
  • LLM/SLM: OpenAI-compatible endpoints; each agent may use its own model.
  • Reranking: local model (ADR-0014).

docs.title: PluginManager (core/plugins/manager.py) — deprecated
docs.text:
• YAML registration — plugin classes listed in config/plugins.yaml and loaded via importlib. (ADR-0001, superseded)
  • Type routing — get_plugin(type) returns the correct initialized plugin.
  • Lifecycle — initialize() → use → close() for clean shutdown.
  • Singleton — global plugin_manager instance.

docs.title: 1. Streamlit UI
docs.text:
• Role: Primary user interface — fetch, browse, search, analysis, knowledge graph, changes tracking, bureaucracy assistant.
  • Pages planned:
  • Fetch Documents (P1) — trigger ETL, upload files
  • Browse Documents (P1) — list, filter, view metadata
  • Search (P1) — keyword + semantic + hybrid, faceted filters (document type, dates, jurisdiction), citations with confidence
  • Analysis (P2) — impact, compliance, citation
  • Knowledge Graph (P2) — visual exploration
  • Changes Tracking (P2) — Git-backed diff-based version comparison
  • Bureaucracy Assistant (P1) — step-by-step administrative procedures
  • Auth: all pages behind streamlit-authenticator (login widget, bcrypt, signed session cookie); RBAC limits data management to admin (users read-only). (ADR-0013, ADR-0004)
  • Frameworks: Streamlit + custom components.
  • No public API — API clients fetch data from the UI/backend directly.

docs.title: 3. Celery + Redis
docs.text:
• Role: Async task queue for long-running operations (document fetching, processing, analysis).
  • Broker: Redis.
  • Result backend: Redis (MVP) → PostgreSQL (production).
  • Tasks: Wrappers around agent methods (e.g., fetch_document, process_document, track_changes).
  • Efficiency: task weights, timeouts, and concurrency tuned for the RAM budget.
  • Reliability (ADR-0006):
  • Retry policies with exponential backoff.
  • Failed tasks persisted to a PostgreSQL failed_tasks table.
  • UI exposes "re-run failed task" for any unprocessed/stuck in-DB task.

docs.title: 4. PostgreSQL (direct, ADR-0014)
docs.text:
• Role: Primary relational store.
  • Stores: Users, tenants, document metadata, text chunks, annotations, processing state, failed-task registry, full-text search index, per-tenant notes/chats.
  • Multi-tenancy: row-level security (RLS) with tenant_id. (ADR-0003)
  • Schema: managed by Alembic migrations — see Migrations.
  • Accessed via: PostgreSQLStore directly.

docs.title: 5. Qdrant
docs.text:
• Role: Vector store for semantic search.
  • Data: Document chunk embeddings.
  • Multi-tenant: collection/partition per tenant.
  • Integration: direct client (ADR-0014; VectorDBPlugin deprecated).

docs.title: 6. Neo4j AuraDB (cloud-managed)
docs.text:
• Role: Graph store for cross-reference tracking.
  • Data: Law articles and their relationships (amends, refers-to, depends-on, cited-by).
  • Hosting: Neo4j AuraDB Free tier. (ADR-0002)
  • Integration: direct client (ADR-0014; GraphDBPlugin deprecated).

docs.title: 7. Embedding, Reranking & LLM
docs.text:
• Embedding — dedicated embedding provider (may differ from the LLM provider); chosen by evaluation on Polish legal texts. (ADR-0009)
  • Reranking — local model (ADR-0014).
  • LLM/SLM — OpenAI-compatible endpoints; each agent may use its own model (ADR-0014).
  • OCR — model chosen by evaluation on Polish documents; runs inside DocumentFetcherAgent under the RAM budget.

docs.title: Observability (ADR-0005)
docs.text:
• Logs: structlog emitting JSON; PII is stripped at the source (anonymized).
  • Metrics: counters/histograms (task duration, queue depth, search latency, error rates) exported via OTel.
  • Traces: OpenTelemetry distributed tracing across UI → Celery → agents → integrations.
  • Export path: OTel → Grafana Alloy → Grafana Cloud.
  • Privacy: no tenant/user identifiers, document content, or query text in telemetry; tenant ID is hashed.
graph LR
    UI[Streamlit] -->|OTel SDK| Alloy[Grafana Alloy]
    Celery[Celery workers] -->|OTel SDK| Alloy
    Agents[Agents] -->|OTel SDK| Alloy
    Alloy --> Cloud[Grafana Cloud]
    Logs[structlog JSON] --> Alloy

docs.title: Security (ADR-0004 / ADR-0013)
docs.text:
• Authentication: streamlit-authenticator login/logout widgets with signed session cookies; credentials come from the PostgreSQL user store (bcrypt-hashed passwords), with a bundled dev admin fallback. (ADR-0013)
  • Authorization (RBAC):
  • admin — manages data: ingest documents, edit/delete, manage users.
  • user — read-only: search, browse, query, view diffs.
  • Enforced in a shared auth/RBAC layer (core/security/) used by the UI and agents; tenant context (tenant_id) is threaded from the authenticated session into the contextvar and query paths.
  • Multi-tenant isolation: tenant_id enforced in every query path (PostgreSQL RLS, vector collection partitioning, graph subgraphs).
  • Automated leak tests assert cross-tenant access is impossible. (ADR-0003)

docs.title: Document Ingestion
docs.text:
Source (PDF / DOCX / HTML / Web / Git)
         │
         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐
  │ ETL Source   │  ← Web ETL / Git ETL
  │ Module       │
  └──────┬───────┘
         │ raw text
         ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ DocumentFetcher  │  ← Agent (via Celery task) + OCR
  │ Agent            │
  └──────┬───────────┘
         │ LegalDocument
         ▼
   ┌──────────────────┐
   │ PostgreSQLStore  │  → PostgreSQL (save document metadata)
   └──────┬───────────┘
         │
         ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ DocumentProcessor│  ← Agent
  │ Agent            │
  └──┬───────┬───────┘
     │       │
     ▼       ▼
  Embedding   Graph
  (direct)   (Neo4j)
     │           │
     ▼           ▼
   Qdrant     Neo4j      PostgreSQL
  (vectors)  (graph)    (chunks)
  1. ETL source module fetches raw text from the source (web, Git, file, API).
  2. DocumentFetcherAgent runs OCR if needed, wraps the result in a LegalDocument model, and persists it via PostgreSQLStore.
  3. DocumentProcessorAgent chunks the text, generates embeddings via the embedding provider, stores vectors in Qdrant, and builds graph edges in Neo4j.

docs.title: Multi-Tenant Isolation
docs.text:
• Shared document storage — documents live in shared tables/collections; access is scoped by tenant_id.
  • Per-tenant state — notes, states, chats, and annotations are isolated per tenant.
  • PostgreSQL: row-level security (RLS) keyed on tenant_id.
  • Qdrant: collection or partition per tenant.
  • Neo4j: subgraph per tenant (label-based).
  • Tenant context is threaded through agents and the data store via the tenant_id field and enforced by middleware.
  • Leak tests (ADR-0003): automated tests assert no cross-tenant read/write.

docs.title: Migration Paths
docs.text:
1. PostgreSQL schema — managed by Alembic migrations; see Migrations.
  2. Plugin → direct integration — each deprecated plugin type (VectorDB, GraphDB, LLM, Embedding, Reranking, KnowledgeSource) is replaced by a direct client as its integration lands. (ADR-0014)
  3. Manual → Automated legal updates: Celery Beat schedule replaces manual triggers.

docs.title: Project Intention
docs.text: Status: Completed — all clarification questions answered. This document now serves as the project charter. Rev. 3 — incorporates the plugin deprecation and hardcoded PostgreSQL direction (ADR-0014); Rev. 2 covered ADRs 1–11.

docs.title: 👁️ Vision & Purpose
docs.text:
1. Elevator pitch – A self-hosted AI assistant that gives legal information, helps protect citizens' rights, and assists with local bureaucracy. It does not give legal advice (ADR-0015).

2. Pain point – Civil-human-rights, family and private law, and daily routine tasks that require legal assistance.

3. Primary target user – EU (Poland) citizens and expats.

4. Project type – Open-source community tool plus a personal research project.

5. North-star metric – Time and money saved per user while tracking legal changes and protecting rights.

6. Scope boundary – The system will not bypass or trick the law.

7. Efficiency mandate – The application must run fast on ~4–6 GB RAM with a small local model (SLM). Efficiency is a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have. Every architectural choice (plugin type, model size, task queue) is made with this budget in mind.

docs.title: ⚖️ Legal Domain Scope
docs.text:
8. Jurisdictions – Poland (EU).

9. Areas of law – Family, child care, taxes, anti-xenophobic law.

10. Source material – All legal material (legislation, case law, commentaries, contracts, procedural documents, etc.).

11. Legal-updates handling – Manual fetching at the beginning.

12. Supported formats – All (PDF, DOCX, HTML, scanned images → OCR, plain text).

13. Cross-reference tracking – Yes – a graph database is required.

14. OCR model – Selected by evaluation on Polish documents (e.g., Tesseract, EasyOCR, PaddleOCR candidates). The chosen model must fit the 4–6 GB RAM budget.

15. Citations – MUST be in the MVP — every search/analysis result must include exact law article citations with confidence scores and direct source links.

docs.title: 📐 Architecture & Technology
docs.text:
16. Deployment model – Docker-Compose (self-hosted).

17. Vector database – Qdrant. (ADR-0014)

18. Graph database – Neo4j AuraDB Free (cloud-managed). (ADR-0002, ADR-0014)

19. LLM provider – OpenAI-compatible endpoints; each agent may use its own model (SLM or hosted). (ADR-0014)

20. Embedding model – Dedicated embedding provider (may differ from the LLM provider); final model selected by evaluation on Polish legal texts. (ADR-0009)

21. Multi-tenant isolation – Yes, from day 1. Documents are shared storage; per-tenant data (notes, states, chats, annotations) is isolated. (ADR-0003)

22. Expected data volume – All Polish law, including tax and foreign statutes (tens of thousands of documents).

23. Processing model – Celery + Redis (asynchronous batch processing) with efficient tasks, retry policies, and in-DB task monitoring so users can re-run failed tasks. (ADR-0006)

24. Data access – PostgreSQL is a direct, hardcoded integration (PostgreSQLStore) with schema managed by Alembic migrations. The plugin system is deprecated. (ADR-0014)

25. Observability – MUST in the MVP: structlog (JSON logs) + metrics + traces via OpenTelemetry, shipped through Grafana Alloy → Grafana Cloud. All telemetry must be anonymized (no PII). (ADR-0005)

26. Health checks – Every container exposes a health check endpoint for monitoring and orchestration. (ADR-0010)

27. Security – streamlit-authenticator auth (MUST) + RBAC: an admin manages data, a user can only read it. Multi-tenant isolation is enforced and tested with leak tests. (ADR-0004 / ADR-0013)

28. SLAs – Basic SLA standards are defined and tracked (search latency, processing time, availability). (ADR-0011)

docs.title: 🔍 Search & Retrieval
docs.text:
29. Search modes – Keyword, semantic, and hybrid (all three).

30. Cross-language search – Supported (e.g., English queries against Polish legal texts).

31. Retrieval strategy – Hybrid RAG with re-ranking, graph-guided multi-hop retrieval.

32. Citation & confidence – MUST in the MVP — confidence scores and exact law article citations with direct source links.

33. Faceted filters – MUST in the MVP — by jurisdiction, document type, dates, court, etc.

34. Find similar documents – Feature will be available.

35. Hybrid search precision – Validated with an evaluation on Polish legal queries; precision/recall targets are defined and measured. (ADR-0005 / ADR-0009)

docs.title: 🤖 Agents & Automation
docs.text:
36. Priority agents – DocumentFetcher (code + OCR), DocumentProcessor (graph manager), LegalResearch, KnowledgeGraph, plus others later.

37. Execution style – Human-in-the-loop (user triggers/approves steps).

38. Change-tracker granularity – Document-level diffs, most likely backed by Git for versioning and comparison. (ADR-0007)

39. Analysis output – Free-text for now.

40. Workflow customization – Pre-configured pipelines (MVP).

41. Bureaucracy/Form Assistant – MUST be in the MVP — a dedicated agent that guides users through administrative procedures step by step.

42. Celery task reliability – Tasks are efficient, failures are persisted in-DB, and the UI lets users re-run failed tasks. (ADR-0006)

docs.title: 🖥️ User Interface
docs.text:
43. Primary UI – Streamlit (as used in existing issues).

44. Public API – No built-in API server; API clients will fetch data from the UI/backend directly.

45. Visualizations – Knowledge-graph, citation network, and timeline visualizations (planned, not in MVP).

46. Annotation & comments – Not needed now; may be added in future versions.

47. Collaboration – Not required at present.

docs.title: 🔐 Security
docs.text:
48. Authentication – streamlit-authenticator (MUST) for all users: login widget, bcrypt-hashed passwords, signed session cookie. (ADR-0013)

49. Authorization – RBAC (MUST): admin role can manage data (ingest, edit, delete); user role is read-only.

50. Multi-tenant isolation – Enforced at every layer: - PostgreSQL — row-level isolation with tenant_id (shared document store, per-tenant notes/states/chats). - Qdrant — collection or partition per tenant. - Neo4j — subgraph per tenant.

51. Tenant leak tests – Automated tests assert that no tenant can access another tenant's data. (ADR-0003)

docs.title: 📈 SLA Standards (basic)
docs.text:
52. Search latency – Hybrid search responds within target latency (e.g., < 3 s for MVP on the 4–6 GB budget); measured and reported via OTel.

53. Document processing – Ingest → chunk → embed → graph completes within a defined processing budget; tracked per task.

54. Availability – Docker-Compose with health checks; service health is visible via the OTel/Grafana stack.

Detailed targets live in ADR-0011.

docs.title: 🚀 Delivery & Timeline
docs.text:
55. Minimum Viable Product – Data collection, processing, annotation, push to PostgreSQL (schema via Alembic migrations), vector store (Qdrant), graph store (Neo4j AuraDB), citations with confidence, filters, document diffs, bureaucracy assistant, and answering complex questions / internal data research — all on the 4–6 GB RAM + SLM budget.

56. Target timeline – MVP: planning date 2027-02-28. If work overruns, the date moves and the scope stays. v1: the date is set after the MVP.

57. Long-term vision – A legal-AI platform for personal and family use, with the possibility of a free online service or bot for answering questions and a legal-tracker component.

docs.title: 🛠️ Meta
docs.text:
58. License – MIT.

59. Contributions – Invite-only (initially).

60. Documentation language – English now; later Ukrainian and Polish.

61. ADR tracking – All significant architecture decisions are tracked as ADRs in Architecture & ADRs.

The charter above defines the scope, technology stack, and roadmap for "Law by AI". All subsequent design, implementation, and testing decisions should be aligned with these constraints and goals.

docs.title: Database Migrations
docs.text: PostgreSQL schema is managed with Alembic. Models live in plugins/relational_db/postgres.py (Base.metadata); migration scripts live in migrations/versions/. The migration environment reads the owner database URL from config.settings (POSTGRES_OWNER_URL, or LAWBYAI_OWNER_PASSWORD and POSTGRES_*).

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Run through uv (the project's package manager):

Task Command Apply all pending migrations uv run alembic upgrade head Apply up to a specific revision uv run alembic upgrade <rev> Undo the last migration uv run alembic downgrade -1 Undo to a specific revision uv run alembic downgrade <rev> Create a migration from model changes uv run alembic revision --autogenerate -m "describe change" Create an empty migration (manual SQL) uv run alembic revision -m "describe change" Show the current revision uv run alembic current Show migration history uv run alembic history Show heads (tip revisions) uv run alembic heads Stamp an existing DB as up-to-date (no SQL) uv run alembic stamp head

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
1. Change the ORM models in plugins/relational_db/postgres.py.
  2. Generate a migration: uv run alembic revision --autogenerate -m "what changed".
  3. Review the generated file in migrations/versions/ — autogenerate can miss column-level changes.
  4. Apply it: uv run alembic upgrade head.

Note: autogenerate compares against the live database, so run it against a schema that is at the latest revision (upgrade head first).

docs.title: Migrations in the data store
docs.text:
The app does not apply migrations on startup. PostgreSQLStore.initialize() only reads the revision of the database. If the revision is not the head revision, it raises SchemaNotAtHeadError.

Migrations run with the owner connection (POSTGRES_OWNER_URL, user lawbyai_owner). The app role (POSTGRES_URL, user lawbyai_app) cannot change the schema. RLS policies for users/tenants live in the migrations (ADR-0003).

docs.title: Overlapping upgrade runs
docs.text:
Each online run of alembic upgrade head takes a session-level advisory lock with the key 0x6C61775F6D6967 ("law_mig") before it reads alembic_version. When two runs overlap, the second run waits. It then sees head and applies nothing, so each migration runs once.

The run tries pg_try_advisory_lock every 1 s until a deadline. The default deadline is 300 s. Set MIGRATION_LOCK_TIMEOUT_S to change it. The value must be a positive number. If the value is 0, negative or not a number, the run fails before it connects. The error names the variable.

  • If the first try fails, the run logs one line. The line gives the key and the deadline.
  • If the lock becomes free before the deadline, the run takes it at the next try. Then it applies only the missing revisions.
  • The last try runs at the deadline. If the operating system wakes the run a little late and the lock is free at that try, the run takes the lock and continues. The deadline limits the wait for a held lock only.
  • If a lock try fails at or after the deadline, the run fails with a timeout error. The timed-out run applies no revision and does not write alembic_version. Another run can still change it in that time.
  • The timeout error gives the key, the deadline in seconds and the pid of the backend that holds the lock. If that backend ended before the run read pg_locks, the error gives "unknown" as the pid.
  • After a timeout, the process exits with a non-zero code. The one-shot init service then fails, and the services that depend on it do not start.
  • If a poll query fails, for example because the connection is lost, the run raises the database error. The run does not report it as a timeout.
  • When a process dies, PostgreSQL ends its session and frees the lock.
  • Offline mode (--sql) takes no lock and does not read the deadline.

docs.title: Docker / test compose
docs.text:
The init service runs alembic upgrade head with the owner connection, then runs the bootstrap program. Start it before the app services.

The test service runs alembic upgrade head with the owner connection, then runs the tests. The tests truncate tables. Run them in a separate Compose project, so that they use their own volume and not the pgdata volume of your normal stack:

docker compose -p law-by-ai-test --profile test -f docker/docker-compose.yml run --rm test
docker compose -p law-by-ai-test --profile test -f docker/docker-compose.yml down -v

Existing local databases created before Alembic (tables created via create_all) usually hold only local test data. Prefer a fresh volume for them. create_all does not create the RLS policies of the initial migration, and the later revisions change those policies, so the upgrade stops without them.

Adopt such a database only when it matches the initial migration in full: the tables, the users_isolation and tenants_isolation policies, and ENABLE and FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on users and tenants. On such a volume lawbyai_owner does not exist yet. Do these steps in order:

  1. Make sure that the two policies exist and that RLS is enabled. Run this query with psql as the bootstrap superuser, on the app database:
SELECT c.relname, c.relrowsecurity, c.relforcerowsecurity, p.polname
FROM pg_class c
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
LEFT JOIN pg_policy p
  ON p.polrelid = c.oid AND p.polname = c.relname || '_isolation'
WHERE n.nspname = 'public' AND c.relname IN ('tenants', 'users');

The result must have two rows. In each row, relrowsecurity and relforcerowsecurity must be t, and polname must be tenants_isolation or users_isolation. If a row is missing, a flag is f or polname is empty, do not adopt the database. Use a fresh volume. 2. Stamp the initial revision with the bootstrap superuser connection. This creates the alembic_version table: POSTGRES_OWNER_URL=<superuser URL> uv run alembic stamp 4439761c5e40. 3. Upgrade to the revision before the RLS hardening, with the same connection. This creates the objects that the next step expects: POSTGRES_OWNER_URL=<superuser URL> uv run alembic upgrade 77985ac8fa22. 4. Do steps 1 and 2 of "Upgrade an old volume" below. They create the roles and give every object, alembic_version included, to lawbyai_owner. 5. Run uv run alembic upgrade head with the owner connection (step 3 below).

Do not stamp head, because the later revisions would then never run.

docs.title: Upgrade an old volume
docs.text:
The Postgres init script makes the database roles. It runs on a fresh volume only. An old volume has one role, the bootstrap superuser (POSTGRES_USER), and that role owns every object. The new migration stops on such a volume. Use this procedure to move an old volume to the new role model.

The procedure makes three roles:

  • lawbyai_owner runs the migrations and owns every object.
  • lawbyai_app is the role that the app, the worker and the tests use. It owns nothing.
  • lawbyai_auth cannot log in. It owns the login lookup function only.

You cannot use REASSIGN OWNED BY to change the owners. The old owner is the bootstrap superuser, and Postgres does not reassign objects that a superuser owns. The block changes the owner of each object one at a time.

  1. Set LAWBYAI_OWNER_PASSWORD and LAWBYAI_APP_PASSWORD in the shell. Use the values from the Docker env file. Do not write a password in the SQL.
  2. Run the block below with psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 as the bootstrap superuser, on the app database. This option stops psql at the first error. psql reads the two passwords from env with \getenv.
  3. Run uv run alembic upgrade head with the owner URL. Set POSTGRES_OWNER_URL to a URL with the user lawbyai_owner and the owner password.
-- Read the passwords from env, so they are not in the SQL text.
\getenv owner_password LAWBYAI_OWNER_PASSWORD
\getenv app_password LAWBYAI_APP_PASSWORD
-- Keep the statement text (with the password) out of the server log on error.
SET log_min_error_statement = panic;
SET log_statement = 'none';

BEGIN;

-- The same roles, attributes and grants as the init script.
CREATE ROLE lawbyai_owner
  LOGIN NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE
  PASSWORD :'owner_password';

CREATE ROLE lawbyai_app
  LOGIN NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS NOINHERIT NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE
  PASSWORD :'app_password';

CREATE ROLE lawbyai_auth
  NOLOGIN NOSUPERUSER BYPASSRLS NOINHERIT NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE;

GRANT CREATE, USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO lawbyai_owner;
GRANT CREATE, USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO lawbyai_auth;
GRANT lawbyai_auth TO lawbyai_owner WITH INHERIT FALSE, SET TRUE;

-- Give each object to the owner role.
ALTER TABLE tenants OWNER TO lawbyai_owner;
ALTER TABLE users OWNER TO lawbyai_owner;
ALTER TABLE legal_document OWNER TO lawbyai_owner;
ALTER TABLE rejected_document OWNER TO lawbyai_owner;
ALTER TABLE alembic_version OWNER TO lawbyai_owner;
-- The sequence belongs to its table. Keep this line after the table line.
ALTER SEQUENCE rejected_document_id_seq OWNER TO lawbyai_owner;
ALTER FUNCTION users_bump_session_version() OWNER TO lawbyai_owner;

COMMIT;

The block runs in one transaction. If a statement fails, no change stays. If the database has more objects that the superuser owns, change their owner in the same way before you run the migration.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
This page tells you how to run the Docker stack. Run all commands from the repository root.

Set this shortcut first:

COMPOSE="docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml"

docs.title: What runs
docs.text: Service Purpose postgres Stores tenants, users and documents. redis Holds the Celery task queue. It runs Valkey and keeps no data on disk. A restart discards queued tasks and results. s3 Stores document files (S3 API, SeaweedFS). init Runs once on each start. It prepares the schema, the bucket, the tenant and the first admin. app Serves the Streamlit web UI. celery-worker Runs background tasks, such as document fetch and OCR. test Runs the full test suite. It starts only with --profile test.

docs.title: First start
docs.text:
1. Copy the example file and protect it:

    cp docker/.env.example docker/.env
chmod 600 docker/.env

  2. Replace every value that starts with change-me. Init stops with exit code 2 while INIT_ADMIN_PASSWORD, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, MINIO_SECRET_KEY or REDIS_PASSWORD still starts with change-me. Use letters and digits only in MINIO_ACCESS_KEY and MINIO_SECRET_KEY.

  3. Start the stack and check it:

    $COMPOSE up -d --build
$COMPOSE ps -a

  4. Open the app on http://127.0.0.1:8501.

Init creates the schema, the bucket, the tenant and the first admin. It runs again on each up. A second run changes nothing.

The S3 service has no published port. Only the services on the backend network can reach it.

docs.title: Stop
docs.text:
$COMPOSE down

down removes the containers. It keeps the pgdata and s3data volumes, but it discards the queued tasks and results in redis, which keeps no data on disk.

Warning

down -v deletes the pgdata and s3data volumes. All database rows and all stored files are lost. Make a dump first if you need the data.

$COMPOSE down -v

docs.title: Start again
docs.text: $COMPOSE up -d

docs.title: Restart
docs.text:
• Restart all services: $COMPOSE restart.
  • Restart one service: $COMPOSE restart app.

restart does not read docker/.env again. To apply a change to docker/.env or to the compose file, run $COMPOSE up -d. If a service does not change, run $COMPOSE up -d --force-recreate <service>.

docs.title: Rebuild
docs.text:
• Rebuild all images: $COMPOSE up -d --build.
  • Rebuild the app and the worker only: $COMPOSE up -d --build --no-deps app celery-worker.
  • Rebuild without the cache: $COMPOSE build --no-cache. Use it only to debug a stale layer. Each uncached build adds to the Docker build cache.
  • Rebuild the test image: $COMPOSE --profile test build test. A stale test image runs old code.
  • Before you apply a change to the redis image, pause producers, drain pending and active tasks, and save any results you still need. The broker keeps no data on disk, so the restart discards them.
  • After a change to an image pin, pull the images, then start: $COMPOSE pull, then $COMPOSE up -d.

docs.title: Develop
docs.text:
1. Edit the code.
  2. Rebuild the app and the worker: $COMPOSE up -d --build --no-deps app celery-worker.
  3. Read the logs: $COMPOSE logs -f app.

Run the fast tests without Docker:

.venv/bin/pytest -m "not integration"

Run the full suite:

$COMPOSE --profile test run --rm test

Run one-off commands:

$COMPOSE run --rm init
$COMPOSE exec celery-worker celery -A tasks.celery_app inspect ping

docs.title: Run init again
docs.text:
$COMPOSE run --rm init

It is safe to repeat. Init checks the state first and creates only what is missing.

docs.title: Check health and resources
docs.text:
$COMPOSE ps
docker stats --no-stream

Measured limits:

Service Peak memory Memory limit CPUs PIDs Basis s3 377 MiB 496m 1.0 200 One 50 MB multipart upload and download. celery-worker 229 MiB 304m 1.0 200 The same upload, 10 pings. app 54 MiB 256m 1.0 200 Provisional. One browser session only. postgres 58 MiB 128m 1.0 200 Provisional. Light load only. redis 15 MiB 32m 0.5 100 Provisional. Light load only. init not measured 128m 0.5 100 Runs once and exits.

Measured on 2026-11-05. No container was stopped for memory. The steady services add up to 1216 MiB, inside the 2 GiB budget. Re-measure the provisional rows with several sessions and a large database before you rely on them.

To find out if the kernel stopped a container because it used too much memory, run:

docker inspect -f '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' <container>

true means an out-of-memory kill. Increase the limit of that service.

docs.title: Change a password
docs.text:
A change to POSTGRES_PASSWORD in docker/.env does not change an existing database. Do one of these:

  • Change the password in Postgres with ALTER USER, then update docker/.env and run $COMPOSE up -d.
  • Delete the data with $COMPOSE down -v, then start again.

The S3 key pair comes from docker/.env on each start of the s3 service. To change it, update docker/.env and run $COMPOSE up -d.

Init creates the first admin only once. A new INIT_ADMIN_PASSWORD does not change an existing admin. Change that password in the app.

docs.title: Upgrade to Postgres 18
docs.text:
The stack uses Postgres 18. Postgres 18 cannot open data from an older major version. The volume also mounts at /var/lib/postgresql now. If your pgdata volume has older data, do one of these:

  • Delete the data with $COMPOSE down -v, then start again.
  • Dump the data with the old stack (pg_dump). Start the new stack. Restore the dump (psql or pg_restore).

docs.title: Security facts
docs.text:
• Published ports bind to 127.0.0.1 only.
  • The backend network has no internet access. Only app and celery-worker also join the edge network.
  • Containers run as non-root users with all Linux capabilities dropped.
  • The S3 service runs as UID 1000. This UID owns /data in the image.
  • SeaweedFS telemetry is off (-master.telemetry=false). Keep it off.
  • OCR is off by default. When OCR_ENABLED=true, document content goes to the Mistral service.
  • All services use one S3 key pair with admin rights until a scoped key exists.
  • Keep docker/.env at mode 600. It holds every secret of the stack.

docs.title: Restart limits
docs.text: After a host reboot, Docker restarts the containers. It does not wait for the health order. The app and the worker retry their connections. If a service stays unhealthy, run $COMPOSE up -d.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Init exit codes:

Code Meaning Action 0 All steps are done or were done before None 2 The configuration is not valid Read the log. Fix docker/.env. 3 Postgres or S3 did not answer after 5 tries of a step Check $COMPOSE ps and the service logs. 4 A step failed Read the log line with result=failed.

required variable ... is missing a value: Compose found an empty required variable. Set it in docker/.env.

Read-only file system: the container root is read-only. The service writes only to /tmp or to its volume. Add a tmpfs entry for the path in the log, and write the reason as a comment next to it.

docs.title: How to add an ADR
docs.text:
1. Copy the template below into a new file docs/adr/NNNN-title.md.
  2. Assign the next number.
  3. Set status to Proposed.
  4. Add the row to the status table.
  5. When accepted, change status to Accepted and note the decision date.
  6. Link the ADR from the relevant section of the Architecture doc.

docs.title: Template
docs.text:
---
status: proposed
---

# ADR-NNNN: <Title>

## Context

<Why is this decision needed? What problem does it solve?>

## Decision

<What is the decision? Be specific and concrete.>

## Consequences

<What are the trade-offs, risks, and follow-up work?>

## Alternatives Considered

- <Option A> — <why rejected>
- <Option B> — <why rejected>

## Related

- <link to other ADRs, issues, or docs>

docs.title: ADR-0001: Protocol-based plugins with YAML registration
docs.text: Superseded by ADR-0014. PostgreSQL is now a direct, hardcoded integration (PostgreSQLStore) and the plugin system is deprecated for a one-person project. This ADR is kept for history.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The MVP plan originally used ABCs (abstract base classes) with importlib auto-discovery of plugins from a directory. As the architecture matured, we need a plugin mechanism that:

  • lets backends be swapped without touching agent code,
  • keeps the 4–6 GB RAM + SLM efficiency budget (no heavy introspection),
  • makes the active plugin set explicit and reviewable in the repo,
  • avoids fragile auto-discovery and class-hierarchy coupling.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Define each of the seven plugin types as a typing.Protocol in core/plugins/protocols/ (RelationalDB, VectorDB, GraphDB, KnowledgeSource, Embedding, LLM, Reranking).
  • Register concrete implementations in config/plugins.yaml.
  • PluginManager reads the YAML, imports the class via importlib, and routes requests by plugin type.
  • Agents depend only on the Protocol; they never import concrete plugins.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Plugins are duck-typed and easily replaced (Chroma↔Qdrant, Memgraph↔Neo4j, OpenAI↔Ollama).
  • Plugin inventory is explicit in one YAML file (good for ops/review).
  • No inheritance hierarchy — simpler tests via lightweight fakes.
  • Requires runtime validation that a registered class satisfies the Protocol.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• ABCs + auto-discovery — original plan; couples implementations to a base-class hierarchy and hides the active set.
  • Entry-point plugins (packaging) — overkill for a self-hosted monolith.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Architecture — Plugin Architecture
  • Intention #24

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Superseded by ADR-0014 — the relational store became a hardcoded direct integration and the plugin system is being deprecated. The implementation history below is preserved for reference.

Accepted. Implemented in the feat/config-settings-plugins branch: the seven protocol contracts, PluginManager, the config/plugins.yaml registry, and the config.plugins facade shipped together with the config/settings layer. Subsequent hardening followed in a separate change.

docs.title: ADR-0002: Neo4j AuraDB Free as the graph database
Context
docs.text:
Cross-reference tracking requires a graph database. The original plan started with in-process NetworkX and targeted Neo4j/Memgraph later. NetworkX holds the whole graph in process memory and serializes to disk — acceptable for small graphs but not for tens of thousands of legal documents on a 4–6 GB RAM budget.

An earlier version of this ADR chose Memgraph for the MVP and Neo4j for production, both behind a GraphDBPlugin. ADR-0014 deprecated the plugin system and fixed the production stack: Neo4j AuraDB Free, cloud-managed.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Neo4j AuraDB Free is the graph database, for the MVP and for production.
  • It is a direct integration. There is no GraphDBPlugin and no Memgraph.
  • The free tier runs outside Docker Compose, so it adds no container and no local RAM.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Cypher skills and query code carry over to any later Neo4j hosting.
  • No graph container in docker-compose, which keeps the local RAM budget.
  • The free tier has size limits. If the graph outgrows them, the move is to a paid AuraDB tier or self-hosted Neo4j with the same Cypher code.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Memgraph (MVP), Neo4j (production) — two engines and a plugin layer for one real target. Dropped with the plugin system (ADR-0014).
  • NetworkX — simplest but in-process memory and no query language.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• ADR-0014 — fixed production stack
  • Architecture — Graph store
  • Intention #18

docs.title: ADR-0003: Shared document storage, per-tenant state
Context
docs.text:
The platform is multi-tenant from day 1. The original design stored every document, chunk, and user record with a tenant_id, plus separate collections per tenant in the vector store and subgraphs per tenant in the graph store.

Legal documents are largely public/shared reference material; only tenant-owned state (notes, chats, processing states, annotations) is truly private. Fully duplicating documents per tenant wastes the 4–6 GB RAM budget.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Documents are shared storage: a single LegalDocument corpus is read-accessible by all tenants (public legislation, case law, etc.).
  • Per-tenant state is isolated: notes, chats, states, and annotations are keyed by tenant_id and never shared.
  • Enforcement:
  • PostgreSQL — row-level security (RLS) on tenant-owned tables; documents are read-only shared rows.
  • Qdrant — partitions/collections scoped by tenant for embeddings of tenant-private content; shared docs use a shared partition.
  • Neo4j — subgraph per tenant.
  • Automated leak tests assert no tenant can read or write another tenant's state.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Efficient storage and embedding of the shared corpus (embedded once).
  • Clear security boundary: shared vs. tenant-owned data.
  • Requires careful query auditing so tenant_id is never omitted on private tables; leak tests enforce this.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Full per-tenant duplication — simplest isolation but wasteful (embedded copies of every document per tenant).
  • Single shared table, no RLS — not acceptable for privacy.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Architecture — Multi-Tenant Isolation, PostgreSQL
  • Intention #21, #50, #51

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Superseded by ADR-0013. JWT is dropped. The RBAC part (admin and user roles) is retained.

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The platform holds legal data and tenant-private state. Any UI/backend access must be authenticated, and not every user should be able to mutate data. The original plan had no explicit auth story.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Authentication: JWT issued on login; validated on every request and reflected in Streamlit session state.
  • Authorization (RBAC):
  • admin — manages data: ingest documents, edit/delete, manage users.
  • user — read-only: search, browse, query, view diffs.
  • Enforced in a shared auth/RBAC layer (core/security/) used by the UI and agents; tenant context (tenant_id) threaded from the token.
  • Tokens are short-lived; refresh/rotation handled by the auth layer.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Secure-by-default: all pages and operations require a valid token.
  • Clear separation of data management vs. consumption.
  • Adds a user/tenant model and login flow to PostgreSQL and UI.
  • RBAC must be tested (privilege escalation tests) alongside tenant leak tests.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Session cookies only — less flexible for future API/server use.
  • OAuth2/OIDC external IdP — heavier than needed for a self-hosted MVP.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Architecture — Security, Streamlit UI
  • Intention #27, #48, #49

docs.title: ADR-0005: structlog + OTel → Grafana Alloy → Grafana Cloud
Context
docs.text: A fast, self-hosted legal platform needs visibility into task failures, search latency, and queue health — without blowing the RAM budget or leaking sensitive legal data. The original plan had no observability stack.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Logs: structlog emitting JSON, with PII stripped at the source.
  • Metrics & traces: OpenTelemetry SDK in the UI, Celery workers, and agents (task duration, queue depth, search latency, error rates).
  • Export path: OTel → Grafana Alloy (local collector) → Grafana Cloud.
  • Privacy (anonymization): no tenant names, user identifiers, document content, or query text in telemetry. Tenant IDs are hashed; document/query content is excluded entirely.
  • Included in the MVP.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Consistent, queryable JSON logs plus distributed traces for debugging.
  • SLA targets (ADR-0011) become measurable via the Grafana dashboards.
  • Slight CPU/RAM overhead from the SDK and Alloy — kept minimal and accounted for in the efficiency budget.
  • Anonymization is a first-class requirement: any span/log attribute that could carry PII is stripped by convention and tested.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Self-hosted ELK/Loki + Prometheus + Grafana — heavier and more moving parts for the budget.
  • No observability in MVP — unacceptable for reliability goals.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Architecture — Observability
  • Intention #25, #52

docs.title: ADR-0006: Celery retries + in-DB failed-task registry
Context
docs.text: Long-running work (fetch, OCR, chunk, embed, graph build) runs on Celery. With a human-in-the-loop model, a failed task should not be silently lost — the user must be able to see what failed and re-run it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Retry policies: Celery tasks configure exponential-backoff retries with a bounded max_retries; timeouts are tuned to the RAM budget.
  • In-DB failure registry: when a task exhausts retries or is detected as stuck/unprocessed, a row is written to the PostgreSQL failed_tasks table (task id, name, args, error, state, timestamps).
  • Re-run from UI: the Streamlit UI lists unprocessed/failed in-DB tasks and offers a "re-run" action that re-enqueues them.
  • Detection: a periodic sweep compares queued/processing tasks against expected progress to surface stuck tasks.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• No silent data loss; users can recover from transient failures manually.
  • Adds a small DB table and one sweep task.
  • Retry + backoff must be tuned per task type to avoid hammering services on the constrained hardware.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Dead-letter broker queue only — requires manual broker surgery and gives no user-facing recovery.
  • No retries (fail loudly) — poor UX for a human-in-the-loop MVP.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Architecture — Celery + Redis, PostgreSQL
  • Intention #23, #42

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The ChangeTrackerAgent must track version changes of legal documents (document-level granularity per the Intention doc). Legal updates (e.g., an amendment to a statute) need reliable diffing and version history.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Document-level diffs, most likely backed by Git for versioning and comparison:
  • Raw text/parsed versions of each document are stored in a Git repository (one branch/namespace per document or a flat versioned store).
  • ChangeTrackerAgent generates diffs via Git history (git diff) between versions.
  • The UI presents version comparison (changes page) from these diffs.
  • Where Git is impractical (binary/OCR-heavy sources), a structured version table in PostgreSQL stores per-version metadata + precomputed diffs, with Git as the canonical source for text documents.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Reliable, auditable version history with cheap diffs.
  • Reuses well-tested tooling instead of custom diff logic.
  • Adds a Git store container/volume to the deployment.
  • Document-level granularity (not section-level) keeps MVP scope tight.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Pure PostgreSQL JSONB version snapshots — no diff tooling; diffs would be custom and fragile.
  • Section/paragraph-level diffs — more granular but out of MVP scope.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Architecture — ChangeTrackerAgent, Changes Tracking UI
  • Intention #38

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The Intention doc listed several features as "planned". Based on the revised priorities (efficiency-first MVP that delivers real value), some must move into the MVP scope:

  • Search must return citations with confidence — the primary value of a legal tool.
  • Users must be able to narrow results by document type, dates, jurisdiction.
  • The bureaucracy/form assistant is the most user-visible daily-use feature and was explicitly marked as a priority agent.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The following are MUST be in the MVP:

  • Citations: every search/analysis result includes exact law article citations, a confidence score, and a direct source link. Data model gains a Citation entity (law, article, paragraph, confidence, source_url).
  • Faceted filters: search supports filters for document type, dates, jurisdiction, court, etc.
  • Bureaucracy assistant: a dedicated agent (BureaucracyAssistantAgent) that walks users through administrative procedures step by step, backed by the document corpus and RAG.
  • Authentication and RBAC: login, and the admin and user roles (ADR-0013).
  • Tenant isolation tests: tests prove that one tenant never reads or writes another tenant's data (ADR-0003).
  • Observability and health checks: structured logs and traces (ADR-0005), and container health checks (ADR-0010).
  • Human in the loop: agents produce drafts. A person reviews and approves them, and new documents wait for admin approval before users see them.
  • Annotation: users can annotate documents.
  • Information-only answers: every answer follows ADR-0015.

Document diffs (ADR-0007) are not in the MVP critical path.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• MVP scope grows but delivers the core value proposition (saved time/money).
  • Adds a BureaucracyAssistantAgent, citation extraction, and filter UI to Phase 5–6 work.
  • Keeps change-tracking (document diffs) and visualizations out of the critical path.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Citations/filters post-MVP — undermines the north-star metric.
  • Bureaucracy assistant as "later" — contradicts priority-agent status.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• ADR-0003, ADR-0005, ADR-0007, ADR-0010, ADR-0013, ADR-0015
  • Architecture — Search & Q&A, Agents, Data Model
  • Intention #15, #32, #33, #41, #55

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The platform targets Polish legal texts. Embedding and OCR quality directly drive search precision and document ingestion accuracy, yet the original plan picked models without evidence. Hybrid search precision needs a measurable target, and every model must fit the 4–6 GB RAM + SLM budget.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Embedding evals: compare candidate embedding models (e.g., Mistral embed, Gemini-mini embed 2, multilingual Sentence Transformers) on a Polish legal corpus. Choose by accuracy + RAM footprint; results live in evals/.
  • OCR evals: compare OCR models (Tesseract, EasyOCR, PaddleOCR) on Polish scanned documents (diacritics, legal formatting). Choose by accuracy + speed
  • footprint.
  • Rerank evals: reranking runs locally (ADR-0014). Compare BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3, Horizon-Labs/multilingual-reranker-small, and no reranking. Measure recall@5 per query language (Polish, English, Ukrainian) and latency for 20-50 pairs on CPU (target under 500 ms). Print the CPU model with the results. No reranking model enters the code before this eval.
  • Hybrid search evals: build a labeled Polish legal query set; measure precision/recall of the hybrid retriever (FTS + semantic + re-rank + graph). Set and track targets (e.g., recall@10) with a baseline commit.
  • Evaluations are reproducible scripts under evals/, not one-off notebooks.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Model/retrieval choices become evidence-based rather than assumed.
  • Some eval tooling and datasets are required early (Phase 3–4).
  • Baseline numbers feed the SLA targets in ADR-0011.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Skip evals, ship defaults — risks poor Polish retrieval and wasted re-embedding later.
  • Evals post-MVP — re-embedding/re-OCR cost is high; doing it late is expensive.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• ADR-0014 — local reranking
  • Architecture — Embedding & OCR Models, evals/
  • Intention #14, #20, #35

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Docker-Compose runs many services (PostgreSQL, Qdrant, Redis, Celery workers, Streamlit, Alloy). Neo4j runs as cloud-managed AuraDB Free, outside Compose. For SLA tracking and fast failure detection, each service must expose liveness/health.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Every container defines a Docker healthcheck (HTTP endpoint or CLI-based probe).
  • Services expose a health endpoint (Streamlit uses its built-in /_stcore/health; DB engines use their native probes). There is no separate API server.
  • Health state is:
  • visible via docker inspect/Compose status,
  • exported into OTel metrics (service up/down) for the Grafana dashboards,
  • used by Compose depends_on: condition: service_healthy to order startup.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Faster failure detection and cleaner startup ordering.
  • Health metrics feed SLA reporting (ADR-0011).
  • Slight per-container overhead; health checks are kept lightweight.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• No health checks, rely on manual docker ps — too slow for SLA goals.
  • Kubernetes-style probes — overkill for Docker-Compose MVP.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Architecture — Technology Stack, docker-compose
  • Intention #26, #54

docs.title: ADR-0011: Efficiency budget (4–6 GB + SLM) and basic SLAs
Context
docs.text: The platform's north-star value depends on it being fast and cheap to run. The original plan had no hardware budget and no measurable service targets.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Hardware budget: the full stack must operate well within ~4–6 GB RAM using a small local model (SLM). This is a constraint on model choice (embeddings, OCR, LLM), vector store mode, Celery concurrency, and service footprint. Where options differ, the more RAM-efficient choice wins.
  • Basic SLA targets (MVP, tracked via OTel/Grafana):
  • Hybrid search latency: < 3 s p95 on the reference corpus/hardware.
  • Document processing (fetch → OCR → chunk → embed → graph): bounded budget per document, tracked per task in the failed-task registry.
  • Availability: services report healthy via health checks (ADR-0010); observed availability is reported, not contractual.
  • Targets are baselines to be refined after the Phase 3–4 evals (ADR-0009).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Concrete, measurable targets for the efficiency mandate.
  • Some features must be descoped if they break the RAM budget.
  • SLA measurement is built in from the start (OTel → Grafana).

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• No stated budget/SLAs — efficiency remains aspirational and unverifiable.
  • Large-model-first, optimize later — contradicts the mandate.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Architecture — Architecture Principles, Observability
  • Intention #7, #52, #53, #54

docs.title: ADR-0012: MIT license and contribution model
Context
docs.text:
The project charter already states MIT and invite-only contributions (Intention #58–59), a MIT LICENSE file and pyproject.toml metadata exist, but the decision was never formally recorded and the contribution model was never fully specified. The open question was to decide between MIT, Apache 2.0, and AGPL and to define how people contribute.

The platform is a self-hosted, open-source community tool for protecting citizens' rights (EU/Poland) plus a personal research project. Its success depends on wide adoption and trust, and it must stay runnable on the 4–6 GB + SLM efficiency budget with freely swappable open-source backends.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. License: MIT — keep the existing MIT License (LICENSE, SPDX MIT in pyproject.toml). MIT maximizes adoption, is simple for community contributors to understand, and does not constrain self-hosting or backend swapping.
  2. Contribution model:
  3. Access: invite-only during the early implementation phase (Phases 1–4). The project opens to public contributions once v1 is stable, at the maintainer's discretion.
  4. DCO, not CLA: every commit must carry a Signed-off-by trailer per the Developer Certificate of Origin. No separate CLA is required — DCO keeps friction low and works for individual contributors.
  5. License grant: by contributing, contributors agree their contributions are licensed under MIT (recorded in CONTRIBUTING.md).
  6. Process: branches named feature/, fix/, or docs/ referencing the issue; PRs must reference the issue (Closes #N / Refs #N) and pass the ci (ruff lint + format, pytest) and docs (mkdocs strict) workflows. Architecture-impacting changes require an ADR.
  7. Maintainership: single-maintainer review for now; significant decisions are recorded as ADRs.
  8. Code of Conduct: Contributor Covenant 2.1 (CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• MIT maximizes adoption and contribution ease; anyone may fork, redistribute, or reuse the code, including commercially.
  • Risk: a commercial party could offer a hosted version without contributing changes back. This is an acceptable trade-off for a self-hosted citizens'-rights tool where reach matters more than protection; it should be revisited if a hosted service is ever planned.
  • DCO is lightweight and auditable via commit trailers; no per-contributor legal agreement overhead.
  • The invite-only phase keeps early design churn inside the trusted core while the public onboarding path is documented for later.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Apache 2.0 — permissive with an explicit patent grant; friendlier to corporate contributors. Rejected for now: it adds a legal appendix and the project has no corporate contributor needs yet. Can be revisited later.
  • AGPL-3.0 — strongest copyleft; would prevent closed SaaS exploitation. Rejected: it raises adoption and contribution friction, can conflict with permissively-licensed dependencies and the personal-research goal, and MIT is already chosen in the charter.
  • CLA — rejected in favor of DCO (less friction, no separate signing step, better fit for an invite-only community project).

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Intention #58, #59
  • CONTRIBUTING.md
  • CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
  • DCO
  • LICENSE

docs.title: ADR-0013: Use streamlit-authenticator for the core app (replace JWT)
Context
docs.text:
ADR-0004 prescribed JWT-based authentication: short-lived RS256 access tokens, Redis-backed refresh-token rotation, and a framework-agnostic core/security/ token layer. Early implementation (the auth branch) showed this was overkill for the current shape of the product:

  • The UI is a single Streamlit process; there is no public API and no micro-service that needs to validate tokens independently.
  • JWT brought real operational weight: RSA key generation/mounting, token TTL/refresh bookkeeping, a Redis revocation store, and session-refresh plumbing in Streamlit — all for one login page.
  • streamlit-authenticator provides battle-tested login/logout widgets, bcrypt password handling, signed session cookies, and failed-attempt tracking out of the box. (The amendment uses only the cookie.)

Multi-tenant isolation (ADR-0003) is unaffected: tenant_id still threads through the core/security/tenant.py contextvar and is enforced by PostgreSQL RLS / collection / subgraph scoping. The tenant and role are read from the user row in PostgreSQL on every rerun, not from a JWT claim.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Replace the JWT auth layer (auth.py, token_store.py, key management, refresh flows) with streamlit-authenticator for the Streamlit app.
  • Users live in PostgreSQL (users, tenants tables, bcrypt hashes). The amendment below describes the login flow.
  • The UI adapter (ui/components/auth.py) keeps the existing surface: login_form(), logout_button(), require_auth(), get_current_user(), is_admin() / require_admin(), and threads tenant_id into the contextvar after login.
  • RBAC (core/security/rbac.py) and tenant context (core/security/tenant.py) stay as-is; hash_password() / check_password() move to core/security/passwords.py (bcrypt).
  • JWT may return later if a public API or service split requires it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Positive
  • Much smaller security surface: no signing keys, no token store, no refresh machinery.
  • Signed cookie sessions come from a maintained library.
  • The PostgreSQL user store doubles as the single source of truth for credentials (no YAML credential file).
  • Negative
  • Authentication is tied to the Streamlit process; a future public API will need its own auth layer (OAuth2/JWT) — tracked as future work.
  • The authenticator's cookie is a session cookie, not a short-lived token; AUTH_COOKIE_KEY must be a strong secret in production.
  • Multi-tenant: unchanged — RLS policies key on the session-scoped app.current_tenant setting; users/tenants tables are RLS-protected (ADR-0003). Cross-tenant leak tests are not built yet.
  • RBAC: unchanged — admin/user roles still gate UI operations.

docs.title: Amendment (2026-11): login reads one user from the database
docs.text:
The library's login() checks passwords only against an in-memory credentials dict. To use it, the app would have to load every user of every tenant, with their bcrypt hashes, into each Streamlit process. That read crosses tenants, and a deactivated user stays valid until the dict is reloaded. The app therefore uses the library differently:

  • A custom st.form collects email and password. The app reads one user by normalised email (strip().lower()) and checks the password with check_password(). A dummy hash keeps the timing equal when no user exists.
  • streamlit-authenticator is used only for the signed session cookie (CookieModel). The cookie holds the email, never the role or tenant.
  • On every rerun, require_auth() reads the user from PostgreSQL again and derives the role and tenant_id from that row. An inactive user or an invalid role ends the session.
  • Each user row has an integer session_version. Deactivation, reactivation and a password change increment it in the same UPDATE statement that changes is_active or the password hash, so the two changes commit atomically. Login reads the version from the same row as the password hash it verifies. The signed cookie value is <email>|<session_version>. require_auth() rejects a cookie whose version does not equal the current row. A copied cookie therefore stops working for good, also after a reactivation. A login that verified an old password issues a cookie with the old version, which is rejected. The check does not depend on AUTH_COOKIE_EXPIRY_DAYS.
  • Emails are normalised on every write as well as on login. Existing rows are migrated, and collisions are resolved before a check constraint is added.
  • The library's failed-attempt tracking is not used. It counted per session only. A database-backed lockout is future work.
  • There is no bundled dev admin. The database seed creates the first admin.
  • The pre-tenant lookup moves to a SECURITY DEFINER function owned by a dedicated role, with fail-closed RLS policies and a non-superuser app role.
  • AUTH_COOKIE_KEY is required, at least 32 characters, and not the library default. AUTH_COOKIE_NAME and AUTH_COOKIE_EXPIRY_DAYS (at least 1) are settings.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• JWT (ADR-0004) — stateless and service-agnostic, but heavy for a single-process UI; superseded by this ADR.
  • OAuth2/OIDC external IdP — heavier still; revisit only if hosted identity becomes a requirement.
  • Load all users into the library's credentials dict (amendment) — keeps the library's login widget and lockout, but reads every tenant's users and hashes into memory and misses deactivations until reload.
  • Streamlit st.secrets-based DIY login — re-implements what streamlit-authenticator already provides (hashing, cookies, widgets).

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• ADR-0004 — superseded (RBAC retained, JWT dropped)
  • ADR-0003 — isolation model, unchanged
  • Architecture — Security section
  • Intention #27, #48, #49

docs.title: ADR-0014: Hardcoded PostgreSQL integration; plugin system deprecated
Context
docs.text:
The original architecture (ADR-0001) defined seven protocol-based plugin types (RelationalDB, VectorDB, GraphDB, KnowledgeSource, Embedding, LLM, Reranking) with YAML registration and a PluginManager routing layer, so every backend could be swapped without touching agent code.

This project is maintained by one person. Maintaining seven interchangeable abstraction layers for a single production backend each is a real maintenance burden: every new feature must be expressed through the lowest common denominator of a Protocol, every concrete implementation needs protocol validation, and the YAML registry must stay in sync — all for backends we never actually swap. The cost outweighs the benefit.

The relational store has exactly one real production target: PostgreSQL (multi-tenant document store, users/tenants with RLS). The swap path for it does not justify a plugin interface.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. PostgreSQL is a hardcoded, direct integration. The RelationalDBPlugin protocol indirection is removed; agents, UI, and tasks import PostgreSQLStore from plugins.relational_db.postgres directly (the UI auth adapter already did this in practice).
  2. The plugin system is deprecated. No new plugin types or routing entries are added. Existing protocol/manager code stays in the tree, marked deprecated, and is removed incrementally as each integration is converted to a direct dependency. No relational_db entry may be registered in config/plugins.yaml again.
  3. Fixed production stack (single provider per concern):
  4. PostgreSQL — relational store, schema via Alembic migrations
  5. Redis — Celery broker / result backend
  6. Neo4j AuraDB Free — graph database (ADR-0002, cloud-managed)
  7. Qdrant — vector store
  8. Grafana Cloud (free tier) + Grafana Alloy locally — observability (ADR-0005)
  9. OpenAI-compatible endpoints for LLM/SLM — each agent may use its own model
  10. Local reranking model — runs on the host (see Amendment)
  11. Embedding provider may differ from the LLM provider

docs.title: Amendment: local reranking
docs.text:
Reranking runs locally. Cohere is dropped from the fixed stack, so no query or document chunk leaves the host for this step. This keeps the 4-6 GB RAM budget and removes one paid external service.

  • The model is chosen by an evaluation (ADR-0009). Candidates are BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3 (int8 ONNX, Apache-2.0) and Horizon-Labs/multilingual-reranker-small (int8 ONNX, Apache-2.0). The evaluation also includes a run without reranking.
  • The evaluation measures recall@5 per query language (Polish, English, Ukrainian) and latency for 20-50 pairs on CPU.
  • No reranking model enters the code before the evaluation.
  • If the model is missing or fails to load, search returns an explicit error. There is no silent fallback.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Simpler code: no Protocol validation, no YAML routing for the relational layer; agents call the store directly.
  • Faster iteration for a single maintainer.
  • Backend swaps (if ever needed) require code changes rather than a config change — accepted trade-off for a one-person project.
  • The other six plugin types are retained only as deprecated scaffolding until their direct integrations land.
  • Migration work is now the single source of truth for the PostgreSQL schema.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Keep all seven plugins (status quo) — high abstraction cost, no real swap benefit for a one-person project.
  • Keep only RelationalDBPlugin, hardcode the rest — half-measure; the same maintenance argument applies to every type with a single backend.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• ADR-0001 — plugin system (now superseded)
  • ADR-0002 — Neo4j AuraDB
  • ADR-0003 — RLS isolation
  • Migrations guide

docs.title: ADR-0015: Answers are legal information, not legal advice
Context
docs.text:
The platform answers legal questions for citizens and expats in Poland. The charter sets one boundary: the system does not bypass or trick the law. The charter also describes the product as an "AI lawyer". That wording suggests that the system gives advice and takes responsibility for the result.

A language model can produce fluent answers that are wrong or out of date. A user may act on such an answer. The product needs an explicit output contract that states what the system is, what it must not do, and how it shows the limits of its answers.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Answers are information only. The system explains laws, procedures, and documents. It does not give legal advice, and it does not replace a qualified lawyer. The user decides and acts.
  2. Every answer shows a notice. The notice states that the answer is information, may be incomplete or outdated, and is not legal advice. The UI shows it next to each answer from the research, analysis, and bureaucracy features.
  3. Every answer rests on sources. An answer includes the citations, confidence scores, and source links defined in ADR-0008. If the confidence is below the set threshold, or no citation supports the answer, the user sees "no reliable answer" and the closest sources. The threshold is a setting. An evaluation tunes it.
  4. The system does not help to bypass the law. It refuses requests to evade, hide from, or trick a legal obligation or authority. The bureaucracy assistant guides only lawful procedures.
  5. A person stays in the loop. The assistant produces drafts of forms and letters. The user reviews them and submits them. The system never submits anything for the user. This follows the human-in-the-loop model of the agents.
  6. Product wording matches the contract. The charter, the documents, and the UI do not present the system as a lawyer or as a replacement for one.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Clear expectations for users and clear limits for the model output.
  • The notice and the refusal rule need prompt design, UI work, and tests. Tests include requests that try to bypass the law and queries with no supporting source.
  • Some questions get a "no reliable answer" reply with the closest sources instead of a fluent guess. This lowers the apparent coverage and raises trust.
  • The charter pitch ("AI lawyer") must change to match item 6.
  • This ADR does not give legal certainty. The owner may need a legal review of the notice text before release.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Position the product as legal advice - needs lawyer supervision and liability cover. It is out of reach for an open-source project run by one person.
  • No explicit contract - leaves the limits to each prompt and each page. The behavior drifts and cannot be tested.
  • Answer from model memory when confidence is low - raises coverage but produces unsupported legal claims.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• ADR-0008 - citations, confidence, source links
  • ADR-0003 - isolation of user data
  • Intention #1, #6, #15, #32, #37, #41
  • Architecture - Agents Layer

docs.title: ADR-0016: Registry and strategy design for the document fetcher
Context
docs.text:
The Document Fetcher agent gets legal documents from several sources. Each source has its own base URL and its own transport. Some sources offer a REST API. Some sources have only web pages. Some documents arrive as files in object storage. The documents come in many formats, and some are scans.

The code needs a clear way to add a source, to choose a transport, and to read a format. ADR-0014 deprecated the plugin system, so the design must not bring it back. The project has one maintainer. The design must stay small, typed, and easy to review.

The fetcher downloads data from remote hosts. A source URL can point to an internal host. A remote host can send a very large or very slow body. The design must limit these risks.

OCR raises a privacy question. A scanned document has no text layer. A hosted OCR service reads the document content. That content then leaves the self-hosted deployment.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Strategy pattern for transport. A FetchStrategy Protocol defines the transport: list references, read metadata, read bytes. Three strategies implement it: REST API, Tavily, and MinIO bucket. A Protocol fits because the strategies share no state.
  2. One hardcoded class per legal source. Each source class declares its name, its base_url, and its strategy_name in code. The base_url must use HTTPS and must not contain credentials. The class returns raw bytes. It does not parse them.
  3. Decorator registry. A generic Registry[T] lives in a module that imports nothing from the project. A source registers itself with @SOURCES.register("name"). A strategy does the same with STRATEGIES. A new source needs no edit to a central list.
  4. The registered name equals the module file name.
  5. A duplicate name fails at import time.
  6. A validation hook checks each source class when it registers.
  7. Module-level instances. The registries (SOURCES, STRATEGIES) sit next to their base classes. They are plain module-level objects. They are not class-level singletons.
  8. Autoload. Each package imports its own modules with pkgutil, so the decorators run. The loader skips base and names that start with _. It fails if a module does not register its own file name.
  9. Format parsers. Parsers for each file format register in the same way. They turn raw bytes into text. They enforce limits on page count, archive size, compression ratio, nesting depth, and text length.
  10. OCR through OcrManager. All OCR goes through one OcrManager. It has one provider: Mistral Document AI. OCR is off by default. When OCR is off, an image or a scanned input raises a typed OcrDisabledError. It is an error, not a result. The system does not read the scan locally, and nothing leaves the host. The ocr/ package is a leaf package. It imports nothing from the other fetcher packages. A later ADR may add another provider (a local model or a gateway) without a change in the callers.
  11. No local folder strategy. The fetcher does not read paths from the local file system.
  12. REST mapping. A source registers a small mapper in a REST_MAPPERS registry, keyed by source name. The REST strategy stays generic. The mapper turns the payload into the fetch contracts. It can declare id safety, an id pattern, and alternative content paths.
  13. Tavily policy. Tavily uses map to list and extract to read. It does not use crawl. Each call has a cap on pages. An empty key is an error.
  14. MinIO and base_url. MinIO ignores the https:// rule on base_url. The endpoint, the bucket, and the credentials come from Settings. Only the path of base_url is the key prefix.
  15. Agent lifecycle. The agent keeps one strategy for each source. It has a close() method, and it works as a context manager. The caller uses close() to release the strategies.
  16. Tenant id. The agent validates tenant_id against [A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}. It rejects any other value.
  17. Network safety. The REST strategy resolves the host at request time. This applies to the first URL and to every redirect. It rejects the request unless all resolved addresses are global. Loopback, link-local, and private addresses fail this check. A source can opt out with allow_private_hosts. The connection is not pinned to the checked address. A host can change its address between the check and the connection (DNS rebinding). The project accepts this risk.
  18. Size and time limits. FETCH_MAX_BYTES limits the size of a fetched body for every strategy. A larger body raises ResponseTooLargeError. FETCH_TOTAL_TIMEOUT is a total deadline for reading a body. A slow body stops when the deadline ends. OCR_MAX_BYTES limits the input size for OCR.

docs.title: Privacy consequence
docs.text:
When OCR is on, the document content goes to a third-party service outside the self-hosted deployment. This breaks the "no document content leaves the host" property that the stack has otherwise.

  • The operator must opt in. The default stays off.
  • The operator must check the legal basis for the transfer before enabling OCR. This includes personal data in the documents.
  • The setting must be visible to the operator in the configuration and in the UI.
  • Document content must not appear in logs, with OCR on or off.

This ADR does not give legal certainty. The owner may need a legal review of the transfer before release.

docs.title: Relation to ADR-0014
docs.text:
The registry is a direct, internal pattern for fetch sources. It is not the plugin system that ADR-0014 deprecated.

  • There is no YAML registration and no Protocol validation of backends.
  • PluginManager is unchanged. It gains no types.
  • The new code does not import core.plugins or plugins.
  • The fetcher does not import PostgreSQLStore. Persistence is a separate step.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• To add a source, a developer adds one file and one test.
  • A source module that fails to import breaks the start of the agent. This is intended. A broken source must not stay hidden.
  • The sources are reviewed in code and typed. The registry check at import time catches wrong names, non-HTTPS URLs, and unknown strategies early.
  • Source configuration is not editable at run time. A change needs a code release. This is an accepted trade-off for a single maintainer.
  • OCR is limited to one provider at first. Users who turn it off cannot read scanned documents.
  • Tavily has a cost and a rate limit. The page cap limits the cost per call.
  • The DNS rebinding window stays open until the connection is pinned to the checked address.
  • A source that opts out of the address check removes the protection for that source. A reviewer must approve each opt-out.
  • Open point: the Tavily daily credit budget.
  • Open point: the retention rule for rejected documents.
  • Open point: the review of the Mistral data-retention terms.
  • Open point: the OCR model pin.

docs.title: Alternatives Considered
docs.text:
• Local folder strategy - rejected as unsafe. A path from a source or from a user can reach files outside the intended folder. It adds a path-traversal risk for little value.
  • Per-source YAML configuration - rejected. The sources are few, reviewed in code, and typed. YAML brings back the registration layer that ADR-0014 removed, and it moves errors from import time to run time.
  • Class-level singleton registry - rejected. Hidden global state makes tests depend on each other. Module-level instances next to the base classes are simple, and tests can use a private Registry.
  • Inheritance for strategies - rejected. The strategies share no state, so a Protocol is enough.
  • Pin the connection to the checked address - not done now. It closes the DNS rebinding window, but it adds transport code that the project must maintain.

docs.title: ADR-0017: SeaweedFS as the S3 object store
Context
docs.text:
The document fetcher (ADR-0016) has a MinIO strategy. It reads documents from an S3 bucket through the Python minio SDK. The first-start init also needs an S3 store. The compose stack has no S3 service yet. The first plan was to run the MinIO community image.

MinIO community edition is no longer a safe base:

  • MinIO stopped publishing community images on Docker Hub and Quay in October 2025.
  • The upstream repository shows "no longer maintained" and is read-only. The repository banner gives 2026-04-25 as the archive date. One aggregator says February 2026. This conflict is not resolved.
  • The last upstream release is RELEASE.2025-10-15.
  • A tutorial dated 2026-01-28 confirms that the images do not get updates. It says that the old Quay examples still run.
  • On 2026-11-05, an anonymous pull of minio/minio from Docker Hub failed (repository missing or needs authorization). Quay returned 401.

The stack must fit in 4-6 GB RAM. The data is a few GB of legal PDFs on a single node.

docs.title: Spike
docs.text:
